newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rich dismiss Jewish woes, pour cash into Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: Rich dismiss Jewish woes, pour cash into Swiss banks.

text.p: The reaction of the world's super-rich to the moral grilling facing Swiss banks over lost Jewish funds has been straightforward -- shrug it off, keep on investing and watch the profits soar.
The secluded, lavishly decorated waiting rooms of turn-of-the-century bank offices in Geneva are full of clients, and the talk so far is of hiring more staff and expanding.

Swiss bankers said the controversy over dormant Jewish accounts has had little impact on the thriving private banking business, with managed asets growing by an estimated 10 percent in the first four months of 1997 after some 25 percent in 1996.

"For fifty years, nobody was ever interested in looking at our archives. Suddenly, you have people grabbing papers out of New York and asking political questions. We were caught with our pants down," said Charles Pictet, partner at Pictet & Cie, Switzerland's leading private bank.
"The reason is we Swiss are bad at communication. Our banks, politicians and the government are completely out of it."
But Pictet said the crisis had had no impact on business.
"I had capacity unemployed last September. Today, we're working at 105 percent capacity," he said. "Demand is so high we have to hire more people."

Dizzying returns on markets this year have contributed to about half of the asset growth, including a jump of more than 20 percent jump in the market capitalisation of Swiss shares alone, with new money making up for the remainder, bankers said.

"There's no business lost as far as we can see," said Pierre Poncet, managing partner at Bordier & Cie, one of Geneva's oldest private banks founded in 1844. "There's more money coming in, and there's more money being saved in Switzerland."
Switzerland, with an estimated 40 percent of offshore wealth, does not publish data on the industry, a by-product of its culture of bank secrecy, and bank reports give only scanty information.
But mutual fund data show an ever-growing mountain of liquid assets.
Statistician Bopp ISB said this month that investors had poured in $11.2 billion into Swiss mutual funds in net flows in the 12 months to end of March and a total $170 billion so far.
"Money just keeps coming in. It's crazy," said Hans Kaufmann, private banking analyst at Bank Julius Baer. "Despite all this talk about Holocaust, I don't see any damage."
At the three Swiss banking giants, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), Credit Suisse and Swiss Bank Corporation (SBC), private banking contributes to more than half of profits, bankers say.
In Geneva, too, private banking remains a cash cow and continues to generate regular, steady revenues despite tough competition and growing downward pressure on fees, bankers said.
Unlike the three top Swiss banks, whose big U.S. businesses could be hurt by the publicity over Jewish funds, bankers in Geneva said they had little exposure to U.S. clients.

Poncet, who estimated that managed assets grew 10 percent in the first four months of the year, said growth was being fuelled mainly by new wealth from emerging countries in the Far East and Latin America.
Patrick Odier, partner at Lombard Odier & Cie, said inflows were also continuing from Germany and traditional continental European clients while that from the Middle East had slowed.
"This has been a happy period," he said.
Bankers said the ultimate questions raised by the crisis over Swiss involvement in the laundering of Nazi gold and the dormant Jewish assets were not about money but about morality.
"The way we say 'rules protect me, I can't answer your questions' will change in the future," said Odier.

"This will have an impact on the behaviour of some banks in Switzerland to act on justified causes. We've all been too close to the letter of the rule and not sensitive to the spirit of the rule. Our organisations will be much wiser in the future."
--- Reuters Geneva Newsroom 41-22-733 38 31
